title: The repo: ai-agents on npm workspaces

story: A run starts for RH-1234. The orchestrator, the Temporal worker that starts and drives every agent run, opens the run's scope in the broker, the service that holds our GitHub, Jira and Slack keys and makes those calls for the run. The scope is a small JSON object: which repo the run may push to, which branch, and which Slack thread it may post in. Last week someone renamed one field in the orchestrator's copy of that object, slackThreadTs became threadTs, because the shorter name read better. The orchestrator's tests passed. The broker has its own copy of the type, which still says slackThreadTs, and its tests passed too.

So CI was green and the change was deployed. Now every run sends a scope that the broker reads as "no Slack thread", and Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, cannot post its plan anywhere. Nothing crashed, nothing was red, and the first person to notice is you, wondering why Slack is so quiet.
hook.question: How do several services in one repo share one definition, so that changing it breaks the build instead of production?

p: The bug in the story has nothing to do with Slack. Two services talk to each other through a shape of data, and each one kept its own description of that shape. A test can only check a service against its own copy, so each test proved that the service agreed with itself. The disagreement lived exactly in the place no test looked: between the two copies.

The fix is to keep one description and let both services import it. In our platform repo, ai-agents, that description lives in a package called shared. It holds the zod schemas for the objects that travel between services, and the broker and the orchestrator both import RunScope from it. A zod schema is both a runtime check and a TypeScript type, so one file answers two questions: what does the compiler allow, and what does the receiver accept?

notes.text: The runtime check. The broker calls RunScope.parse on every scope it receives.
null means the run has no Slack thread, which is a real case, so it is part of the shape.
The TypeScript type, made from the schema. Same name, so one import gives you both.

read.h: Workspaces: import a folder by its name
p: How does the broker import a package that is not on the npm registry? With npm workspaces. The root package.json lists folders, and each folder is a package with its own package.json and its own name, here @rhinohealth/ai-agents-shared. One npm install at the root creates a link in node_modules for each workspace, pointing at its folder. So the broker writes an ordinary package import, Node and TypeScript follow the link, and nothing is ever published.

The link is a symbolic link, not a copy. When you edit shared/src/index.ts, every service that imports it sees the new file immediately, which is exactly what makes a change to it visible everywhere at once.

notes.text: The name other workspaces import. A service lists it in its dependencies as "@rhinohealth/ai-agents-shared": "0.1.0".
The compiler reads the source file, so a typecheck needs no build first. Running code uses the built file in dist/.

p: Sharing one schema only helps if a change to it is checked against every package that uses it. That is the job of the scripts in the root package.json. npm run typecheck --workspaces runs the typecheck script of every workspace, in the order the workspaces are listed, and --if-present skips a package that has no such script. npm also keeps going after a failure, so one run shows every package the change broke.

Replay the story with the shared schema. The rename now happens in shared, because there is no other copy to rename. The same pull request runs the root typecheck, and it fails twice: in the broker, which reads slackThreadTs, and in the orchestrator, which writes it. The author has to fix both in the same pull request, and the broken pair never reaches main.

notes.text: shared comes first, so its scripts run before the packages that use it.
Every workspace's typecheck, one after another.
npm runs pretest by itself before test. Tests import shared's built file, so it is built first.
One test run for the whole repo: tsx runs the .ts test files, and the glob finds test/ in every workspace.

read.see:
> @rhinohealth/ai-agents-broker@0.1.0 typecheck
src/scopes.ts(4,60): error TS2339: Property 'slackThreadTs' does not exist on type '{ runId: string; repo: string; branch: string; threadTs: string | null; }'.
> @rhinohealth/ai-agents-orchestrator@0.1.0 typecheck
src/open-run.ts(7,3): error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'slackThreadTs' does not exist in type '{ ... threadTs: string | null; }'.

deeper.h: Go deeper: why the broker still parses
p: If both services import the same type, why does the broker also call RunScope.parse? Because types disappear when TypeScript is compiled. The scope arrives at the broker as JSON over HTTP, and at that moment it is just bytes. The two services are also deployed one at a time, so for a few minutes a new orchestrator can talk to an old broker. parse turns any mismatch into a clear 400 error that names the field, instead of a quiet undefined that looks like "no thread".

The repo holds every service of the platform: the LLM gateway (our only door to Claude), the broker, the orchestrator, the harness (our program that runs the Claude session inside the agent's VM), the Slack app and shared. Code leaves the repo in only two ways, and both are built from main after the checks pass. The services become Docker images that run on our internal cluster. The harness becomes one bundled file, because the VM should install nothing at run time.
Both outputs inherit the same contract: the shared package is compiled into each image and bundled into the harness file, so every piece of one release was checked against the same schema.

deeper.h: Go deeper: CI, the release and the rules on main
p: CI runs on every pull request and on every push to main, with three jobs: lint (npm ci, lint, typecheck), test (npm ci, test, build) and evals, a small Python project for our benchmark runner. The jobs are separate because a required check is a job name, and you want to see which one is red.

The harness release bundles harness/ with esbuild into one file, nova-worker.mjs, with a two-line banner: the #!/usr/bin/env node line, then a line that creates require, because some packages, such as yaml, still call require inside an ES module bundle (the bundling lesson shows the error you get without it). The release attaches a tarball with that file plus its prompts and settings.

Main has a ruleset: a pull request with exactly one approval, stale approvals dismissed on a new push, the three checks required, no force push and no deletion. Our agents' GitHub App gets no bypass, so an agent can open a pull request in this repo but never merge one, even here, where the walls themselves are written.

lab.title: One schema, three services
needs: Node 22 or newer (the platform uses 24; 22 works for this lab)
About 30 MB of disk for TypeScript, tsx and zod
lab.goal: Build a small copy of the ai-agents workspace where the broker and the orchestrator share one schema, then rename a field and watch one root command point at every place that must change.

guess.q: The broker and the orchestrator both import RunScope from the shared workspace. You rename slackThreadTs to threadTs in shared and run npm run typecheck at the root. What do you expect?

options.text: It passes, because shared itself still compiles.
options.why: shared does compile. But the root runs the typecheck of every workspace, and the other two still use the old name.

options.text: It fails in the broker and in the orchestrator, each at the line that uses the old name.
options.why: Both import the one type through the workspace link, so both see the rename at once. npm keeps going after the first failure, so you get both errors.

options.text: It fails only in the first workspace and stops there.
options.why: npm runs the script in every workspace and reports each failure, which is what you want from a contract check.

follow.say: Create the root of the repo: the workspace list, the root scripts and one shared compiler setting.
follow.do:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/g3-1 && cd ~/academy-labs/g3-1
cat > package.json <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "@rhinohealth/ai-agents",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "workspaces": ["shared", "broker", "orchestrator"],
  "scripts": {
    "typecheck": "npm run typecheck --workspaces --if-present",
    "pretest": "npm run build --workspace shared",
    "test": "node --import tsx --test --test-reporter=spec \"*/test/**/*.test.ts\""
  }
}
EOF
cat > tsconfig.base.json <<'EOF'
{ "compilerOptions": { "strict": true, "target": "ES2023", "module": "NodeNext", "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
  "verbatimModuleSyntax": true, "declaration": true, "skipLibCheck": true, "types": ["node"] } }
EOF
for pkg in shared broker orchestrator; do
  mkdir -p $pkg/src $pkg/test
  echo '{ "extends": "../tsconfig.base.json", "compilerOptions": { "rootDir": "src", "outDir": "dist" }, "include": ["src"] }' > $pkg/tsconfig.json
done
follow.see: (no output: three folders, each with a tsconfig.json)

follow.say: Write the shared package: its package.json from Understand and the RunScope schema.
follow.do: Save shared/package.json and shared/src/index.ts exactly as shown in Understand.

follow.say: Write the two services. Both depend on shared by name, and each has one small test.
Install once at the root, with exact versions, and look at what npm did with the three folders.
follow.do:
npm install --save-exact --save-dev tsx@4.20.3 typescript@5.9.3 @types/node@24.12.2
npm install --save-exact --workspace shared zod@4.6.7
ls -l node_modules/@rhinohealth/

follow.say: Run the root checks while everything agrees.
follow.see:
> @rhinohealth/ai-agents-shared@0.1.0 typecheck
> @rhinohealth/ai-agents-broker@0.1.0 typecheck
> @rhinohealth/ai-agents-orchestrator@0.1.0 typecheck
✔ a run with a Slack thread may post in it (1.06ms)
✔ the scope the orchestrator sends is one the broker accepts (1.01ms)
ℹ pass 2
ℹ fail 0

follow.say: Now make the rename from the story, but in the one place it can happen, and run the same command.
follow.do:
sed -i.bak 's/slackThreadTs: z/threadTs: z/' shared/src/index.ts
npm run typecheck 2>&1 | grep 'error TS'
follow.see:
src/scopes.ts(4,60): error TS2339: Property 'slackThreadTs' does not exist on type '{ runId: string; repo: string; branch: string; threadTs: string | null; }'.
src/open-run.ts(7,3): error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'slackThreadTs' does not exist in type '{ runId: string; repo: string; branch: string; threadTs: string | null; }'.

lab.build: Undo the rename (mv shared/src/index.ts.bak shared/src/index.ts). Add a fourth workspace, slack-app, the way you added the broker: a package.json named @rhinohealth/ai-agents-slack-app that depends on shared, a function threadLink(scope) that returns a Slack link built from scope.slackThreadTs or null, and one test. Add slack-app to the root workspaces list (npm pkg set 'workspaces[3]=slack-app') and run npm install again. Then rename the field in shared once more and count the errors.
checks: node_modules/@rhinohealth/ has one link per workspace, and each one points at a folder, not a copy.
npm run typecheck prints a typecheck line for every workspace, shared first.
With the field renamed in shared, the typecheck fails in the broker and in the orchestrator at the lines that use the old name.
After you add slack-app, npm test shows 3 passing tests, and the rename makes slack-app fail too.
Nothing in your workspace was published or downloaded under the @rhinohealth name: npm ls @rhinohealth/ai-agents-shared shows it as a link (->).

solution.file: slack-app/src/thread-link.ts (plus a package.json and tsconfig.json like the broker's)

lab.fix: A teammate wanted the orchestrator to build without the shared package, so they pasted a copy of RunScope into orchestrator/src/open-run.ts and deleted the import. Recreate it: replace the import line with a local type RunScope = { runId: string; repo: string; branch: string; slackThreadTs: string | null }. Rename the field in shared and fix the broker. Now the typecheck is green, but npm test fails with invalid_type on threadTs. Find why the typecheck could not warn you, delete the copy, import the type from shared again, and let the typecheck show you the line to change.
explain: Why did both services pass their own tests in the story, even though they could not talk to each other?
What does npm install put in node_modules for a workspace, and why does that make a change in shared visible to every service at once?
If both services import the same type, why does the broker still call RunScope.parse on what it receives?
lab.done: A rename in shared makes the root typecheck fail in every workspace that uses the field, and npm test passes again once you fix them all.

check.q: The broker and the orchestrator each keep their own copy of the RunScope type. Someone renames a field in the orchestrator's copy only. What happens?

options.text: The broker's typecheck fails, because the types no longer match
options.why: The broker checks against its own copy, which did not change. Nothing connects the two copies, so nothing fails.

options.text: Both typechecks and both test suites pass, and the mismatch shows up only when the services talk in production
options.why: Each service agrees with its own copy. The disagreement is between the copies, where no test looks.

options.text: npm install refuses to install two types with the same name
options.why: npm knows nothing about TypeScript types. Two copies are just two files.

check.q: Why does the root typecheck use --workspaces instead of checking only the package you changed?

options.text: Because a change to shared can break any package that imports it, so every consumer must be checked in the same run
options.why: The point of a shared contract is that one change is checked against everyone who depends on it, before merge.

options.text: Because npm cannot run a script in one workspace
options.why: It can, with --workspace <name>. The pretest script does exactly that for shared.

options.text: Because it is faster than one typecheck per package
options.why: It runs one typecheck per package anyway. The reason is coverage, not speed.

check.q: Both services import RunScope from shared. Why does the broker still call RunScope.parse on every scope it receives?

options.text: Because zod needs parse to create the TypeScript type
options.why: z.infer creates the type at compile time. parse is a separate check that runs on real data.

options.text: Because parse makes the typecheck faster
options.why: parse runs when the program runs, not when it compiles.

options.text: Because types vanish at run time: the scope arrives as JSON, and a sender from another release could still send the old shape
options.why: During a deploy an old orchestrator can talk to a new broker. parse turns that into a clear error that names the field.

p: The platform repo is RhinoHealth/ai-agents: TypeScript on Node 24, ES modules, npm workspaces shared, gateway, broker, orchestrator, harness and slack-app (checks, metrics and drills come later), each named @rhinohealth/ai-agents-<pkg>, with src/*.ts in kebab-case and test/*.test.ts, and an evals/ folder that is a small Python project managed with uv. The zod schemas that travel between services, such as RunScope, Task, Plan and Charter, live in shared/src/schemas.ts. Byte's style applies: ESLint with typescript-eslint, node:test through tsx, exact pins, few runtime dependencies.

ci.yml runs lint, test and evals on fcp-runner-set. images.yml builds the orchestrator, broker, gateway, slack-app and checks images from node:24-bookworm-slim pinned by digest, non-root user 10001, into inf ECR with immutable tags. release-harness.yml bundles nova-worker.mjs with the two-line banner and attaches ai-agents-harness-<version>.tgz, which the sandbox image unpacks. Main's ruleset: one approval, stale approvals dismissed, lint, test and evals required, no force push or delete, no bypass for rhino-ai-agents, no CODEOWNERS. A short AGENTS.md and a CLAUDE.md that only says @AGENTS.md finish the repo.

tickets.why: Creates the repo: workspaces, the shared package, CI, the images, the harness release and the ruleset on main.
The broker's RunScope is the first contract in shared, read by the orchestrator and the broker.

words.plain: A folder with its own package.json, listed in the root package.json and linked into node_modules by its name.
The workspace that holds the schemas and types every service imports, so there is only one copy.
The shape of data two services agree on. If it lives in one place, a change to it is checked everywhere.
A file that points at another folder. Workspaces use it, so edits are seen at once, with nothing copied or published.
A check that runs on real data while the program runs, like RunScope.parse, unlike a type, which is gone after compiling.

review.q: Write the root scripts typecheck, pretest and test from memory, and say why pretest exists.
review.a: typecheck: npm run typecheck --workspaces --if-present. pretest: npm run build --workspace shared. test: node --import tsx --test "*/test/**/*.test.ts". Tests import shared's built file, so shared must be built before they run.

review.q: A teammate wants to copy RunScope into the Slack app "to keep it independent". What do you answer?
review.a: A copy cannot fail when the original changes, so the drift reaches production, as in the story. Import it from shared; the workspace link costs nothing and nothing is published.

remember: Keep every shape that travels between services in one shared workspace, and let one root command check every service that uses it, so a change breaks the build instead of production.
